Romantic piano miniatures

Seven collections of Romantic piano pieces, from Chopin to Medtner, set after the Classical-era keyboard sonatas, and three string-quartet collections side by side.

1. The collections

Seven collections of Romantic piano music that DCML analysed under one harmony annotation standard and published: 197 pieces, 17,961 bars. Most are short character pieces (mazurkas, lyric pieces, Kinderszenen); Liszt's Années de pèlerinage has many longer ones. The charts on this page set them after the six dated Classical-era sonata collections of 1.8 (J. C. Bach left out).

2. Keyboard music, 1740–1925

Top to bottom by median year of composition. One dot per movement or piece; vertical bar = median. Click a metric's name for its definition and formula. The last four are new in 1.9.

BeethovenMozartClassical-era sonatasRomantic piano pieces

Pitch range

Distance between the highest and lowest note in the movement.

Chromatic ratio

Share of notes outside the key signature in force in that bar (notes needing an accidental).

Note density

Number of note onsets per quarter-note beat, all parts combined.

Pitch-class entropy

How evenly the twelve pitch classes are used.

Seventh-chord ratio

Share of chords containing a seventh.

Applied-chord ratio

Share of chords applied to another key's tonic (secondary dominants such as V/V).

Modulation rate

Number of changes of the annotated local key, per 100 bars.

Chord vocabulary

Distinct chord labels per 100 labels.

Key clarity

How closely the movement's pitch distribution resembles the typical distribution of a single key (new in 1.9).

Falling-fifth root motion

Share of chord changes in which the root falls a fifth (rises a fourth) (new in 1.9).

Key-change distance

Median number of steps the key signature moves when the local key changes (new in 1.9).

Notes outside five octaves

Share of notes outside the five octaves F1–F6. Keyboard collections only (new in 1.9).

3. What the data show, and what to watch for

A median for each collection; then the median of those medians for the six Classical-era and the seven Romantic collections (one vote per collection; C. P. E. Bach: the 50 sonata movements only). The heatmap below sets the same medians against the mean of the 13 collections (the number in each cell is the median).

  • Chromatic ratio: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 0.112, Romantic 0.144. Among the Romantic collections, highest Liszt (0.234), lowest Schumann (0.086).
  • Pitch-class entropy: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 3.19, Romantic 3.23. Among the Romantic collections, highest Liszt (3.40), lowest Schumann (3.06).
  • Key clarity: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 0.88, Romantic 0.87. Among the Romantic collections, highest Tchaikovsky (0.88), lowest Liszt (0.85).
  • Seventh-chord ratio: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 0.249, Romantic 0.414. Among the Romantic collections, highest Medtner (0.426), lowest Dvořák (0.262).
  • Falling-fifth root motion: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 0.389, Romantic 0.379. Among the Romantic collections, highest Schumann (0.481), lowest Liszt (0.294).
  • Modulation rate: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 4.4, Romantic 6.8. Among the Romantic collections, highest Tchaikovsky (16.7), lowest Grieg (1.2).
  • Key-change distance: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 1.0, Romantic 1.0. Among the Romantic collections, highest Liszt (3.0), lowest Chopin, Schumann, Tchaikovsky, Grieg, Medtner (1.0).
  • Notes outside five octaves: median of the collection medians: Classical-era 0.000, Romantic 0.004. Among the Romantic collections, highest Dvořák (0.010), lowest Chopin, Schumann (0.000).

What to watch for.

  • The Classical-era side is sonata movements, the Romantic side mostly short character pieces. Differences mix period with genre, especially for metrics that can vary with length (modulation rate, chord vocabulary).
  • Chord metrics count harmony labels that people added, so they measure the annotators' judgment as well. The Chopin, Liszt collections use different versions of the standard for different pieces. The Chopin collection has pieces without harmony labels; they drop out of the chord metrics. Key clarity and the share of notes outside five octaves are counted from the notes and do not depend directly on the harmony annotators (score edition and encoding still matter).
  • The five-octave reference (F1–F6) is fixed for comparison; real keyboard compasses differed by period and instrument.
  • The collections are the ones researchers annotated, not a sample drawn to represent the period. Large parts of the repertoire are missing: Chopin's other genres, the piano music of Brahms and Mendelssohn, Schubert's sonatas.

4. Key maps

Each bar is one movement, coloured by the local keys annotated by DCML, from beginning to end. Three pieces per collection, chosen by a fixed rule: the one whose number of key changes is closest to the collection median, the one with the most and the one with the fewest (hover over a piece name to see which). Hover over a segment for its bars, key and signature.

Colour now shows distance from the home key. Keys with the home key's signature (the home key and its relative) are grey, the dominant side (sharp direction) orange, the subdominant side (flat direction) blue, with more contrast against the background the further away (darker on a light screen, lighter on a dark one). Good for comparing the shape of modulation across pieces.Colour now shows the actual key. Keys without accidentals (C major, A minor) are grey; more sharps, stronger orange; more flats, stronger blue. Each piece starts from its own colour. Either way the colours follow the same circle of fifths; only the reference point differs. Colour uses the signature difference without enharmonic folding (F♯ major +6, G♭ major −6); keys beyond six steps take the end step. The metric 'key-change distance' folds enharmonically to 0–6, so it can differ from the number of colour steps. Bar 0 is a pickup bar. Ties in choosing pieces go to the lower piece number.

Keyboard collections

String quartets

Local keys are the DCML annotators'. Another analyst could draw the boundaries of a modulation differently. The colours encode distance on the circle of fifths; they make no claim that a key has a colour of its own. the colour keyboard (clavier à lumières) of Scriabin's Prometheus and the DCML lab's Wavescapes (Viaccoz et al. 2023) also laid out colour along the circle of fifths, and Palmer et al. (2013) report that people associate major with lighter and minor with darker colours. Here a diverging scale of two hues (blue, orange) and grey is used. Orange and blue of the same step are OKLab ΔE 13–20 apart under simulated protanopia and deuteranopia (Machado et al. 2009; target 8 or more). The palest steps (±1) on a light screen differ by only 14.8 even for normal vision, so tooltips and the legend's numbers back them up. No user testing was done. Minor keys are hatched rather than darkened.

  • The three collections use different versions of the harmony annotation standard (Pleyel 2.3.0, Beethoven 1.0.0, Mendelssohn 2.1.0). Differences in chord metrics may mix in differences in the annotation rules, by an amount these data cannot separate.
  • Only the Pleyel collection carries cadence labels, so the two cadence metrics are left out of this comparison.
  • Pleyel has fewer than 10 movements.
